steps.premise: Boards become hard to identify once similar pots accumulate.
steps.action: Keep reusable name cards and a pencil at the rack.
steps.consequence: A maker can mark their board before the neighboring boards fill.
steps.quote: Keep a pencil and reusable name cards by the rack so a maker can claim a board before a dozen similar bowls land beside it.

steps.premise: Some shelves are too deep to reach from the front.
steps.action: Keep the back of those shelves accessible.
steps.consequence: People can reach their work without leaning over fresh pot rims.
steps.quote: If a shelf is too deep to reach across from one side, leave access behind it so nobody has to lean over a row of fresh rims.

steps.premise: A low dish can look like an empty space at the back of a dim shelf.
steps.action: Aim a small lamp along the back.
steps.consequence: Makers can tell which spots are actually free.
steps.quote: A small lamp aimed along the back of a dim shelf makes an empty spot easier to distinguish from a space occupied by a low dish.

steps.premise: Beginners need to judge spacing before they load a board.
steps.action: On the teaching table, show pots spaced far enough apart for a hand to pass.
steps.consequence: Beginners can copy that spacing on their own boards.
steps.quote: Leave an example board on the teaching table with the pots spaced for a hand to pass between them. Beginners can see how much room to allow before they load their own.

steps.premise: A warped or splintered board could be used for a flat platter.
steps.action: Remove damaged boards from the supply as soon as they are spotted.
steps.consequence: The next student can avoid setting a platter on an uneven support.
steps.quote: Take warped or splintered boards out of the supply as soon as someone spots them, before another student sets a flat platter on an uneven base.

steps.premise: A piece may need attention while its maker is away.
steps.action: Let members designate someone to check their work during an absence.
steps.consequence: Staff know whom to ask about the piece.
steps.quote: Let members nominate someone to check their work during an absence, giving staff a known person to ask if a piece needs attention.

steps.premise: The number of chairs available can depend on the date.
steps.action: Show the available count for each date on the shared booking calendar.
steps.consequence: Organizers can tell whether enough chairs are available for their event.
steps.quote: Put the number of available chairs against each date on a shared booking calendar so organizers can see whether a request will fit.

steps.premise: Chairs for an evening event may still be away the next morning.
steps.action: Collect pickup and return times when the organizer books.
steps.consequence: The booking accounts for the full time the chairs will be out.
steps.quote: Ask for the pickup and return times when a booking is made, since a Saturday evening event may mean the chairs are still out on Sunday morning.

steps.premise: A driver who is late may need to reach the person with the keys.
steps.action: Have the organizer name a contact who can be reached during the event.
steps.consequence: The driver knows whom to call.
steps.quote: Have each organizer name someone reachable during the event. A driver running late can call the person with the keys.

steps.premise: A chair with a loose hinge or missing foot could go out in the next delivery.
steps.action: Give it a visible repair tag and store it separately.
steps.consequence: It stays out of the next batch sent to borrowers.
steps.quote: Give a chair with a loose hinge or missing foot a conspicuous repair tag and a separate storage spot, keeping it out of the next delivery.

steps.premise: Returned chairs need inspection and cleaning before another pickup.
steps.action: Leave time between bookings.
steps.consequence: The team can check and clean the batch before the next group arrives.
steps.quote: Allow time between bookings to check and clean a returned batch before another group expects to collect it.

steps.premise: An organizer may have to leave before the return.
steps.action: Allow the borrower to nominate another person to bring the chairs back.
steps.consequence: The chairs can still be returned on time.
steps.quote: Let a borrower nominate another person to make the return so the chairs can get back on time even when the event organizer has to leave early.

steps.premise: Two speakers may talk at once and both be intelligible.
steps.action: In those passages, caption each voice on its own line.
steps.consequence: Visitors can recognize that the remarks overlap.
steps.quote: For overlapping conversation, give the two voices separate lines where both are intelligible. Visitors can see that the remarks were made together.

steps.premise: A visitor may want to judge caption size before a long interview.
steps.action: Put a text-size control at each station and provide a sample caption to try it on first.
steps.consequence: Visitors can choose a readable size before the interview starts.
steps.quote: Provide a text-size control at each station and let visitors try it on a sample caption before starting a long interview.

steps.premise: A visitor needs captions as soon as the first words are spoken.
steps.action: Start each fresh session with captions already visible.
steps.consequence: Visitors can read the opening without searching the settings.
steps.quote: Start a fresh listening session with captions visible so a visitor can read the opening words without searching through settings.

steps.premise: A listener may be interested in one topic in a long interview.
steps.action: Provide a short topic list with jump points.
steps.consequence: The listener can go directly to the passage of interest.
steps.quote: Give long interviews a short list of topics with jump points, letting someone go straight to the passage about the old school or the flood.

steps.premise: A local custom mentioned by a speaker may be unfamiliar.
steps.action: Keep optional background notes in the interview listing.
steps.consequence: Visitors can consult them without losing their place in the sentence.
steps.quote: Keep optional background notes in the interview listing. Visitors can look up an unfamiliar local custom without losing their place in the speaker's sentence.

steps.premise: People may enter a looping exhibit partway through an interview.
steps.action: Display the interview title beside the captions.
steps.consequence: Late arrivals can identify which story they are following.
steps.quote: For an exhibit that plays on a loop, display the interview title alongside the captions so someone arriving midway can place the story.

steps.premise: Guests may be unsure how to invite someone or turn down a dance comfortably.
steps.action: Demonstrate a friendly invitation and a friendly decline during the welcome.
steps.consequence: Guests hear how the exchange can end comfortably with either answer.
steps.quote: Model both a friendly invitation and a friendly decline during the welcome. Guests get to hear how either answer can end comfortably.

steps.premise: A beginner needs a moment to decide whether to join a particular dance.
steps.action: Announce the dance type before starting the music.
steps.consequence: The beginner has time to decide whether to get up.
steps.quote: Announce the type of dance before the music starts so a beginner has time to decide whether to get up for it.

steps.premise: Some dancers find spinning uncomfortable.
steps.action: Show an easier version of the turn with both feet close to the floor.
steps.consequence: They can take part in the figure.
steps.quote: Show an easy version of a turn that keeps both feet close to the floor, giving anyone who finds spinning uncomfortable a way through the figure.

steps.premise: Noise can make a spoken demonstration hard to follow.
steps.action: Light the teacher’s face and feet well during demonstrations.
steps.consequence: Participants can follow the visual cues.
steps.quote: Keep the teacher's face and feet well lit during demonstrations so people can use visual cues when the room is noisy.

steps.premise: Arriving guests need the right fare and a way to pay.
steps.action: List the door price and payment options in the invitation.
steps.consequence: Guests can arrive ready to pay and go straight in to meet the host.
steps.quote: Include the door price and payment options in the invitation so people can arrive with the fare in hand and head straight in to meet the host.

steps.premise: Someone who sits out songs may still want to meet the group.
steps.action: Lower the music during a break and invite a brief chat.
steps.consequence: They can get to know people while off the dance floor.
steps.quote: Invite people to chat briefly over a break with the music turned down. Someone who sat out a few songs can still get to know the group.

steps.premise: Someone living alone may want several kinds without taking more bread than they can eat.
steps.action: Ask bakers to wrap a few small portions of each loaf.
steps.consequence: A visitor can take home a variety without wasting bread.
steps.quote: Ask bakers to wrap a few small portions from each loaf so someone who lives alone can bring home several kinds without wasting bread.

steps.premise: Several selections may be hard to identify once home.
steps.action: Provide paper bags sized for a few slices and a pencil to label them.
steps.consequence: Visitors can tell their breads apart later.
steps.quote: Set out paper bags big enough for a few slices and a pencil for writing on them, so people can tell their selections apart once they're home.

steps.premise: Someone choosing an unfamiliar loaf may wonder how to eat it the next day.
steps.action: Ask each baker how they enjoy their bread the following day, such as reheated or toasted.
steps.consequence: A serving suggestion can make the unfamiliar bread easier to choose.
steps.quote: Ask each baker how they like to eat their bread the following day. A reheating or toasting suggestion makes a less familiar loaf easier to choose.

steps.premise: A child may want to help at the swap.
steps.action: Let the child draw a picture of a loaf for the table.
steps.consequence: Families can participate together without handling the samples.
steps.quote: A child who wants to help could draw a little portrait of a loaf for the table, giving families something to do together without handling the samples.

steps.premise: Spare bread may need a destination at closing.
steps.action: Invite contributors to choose in advance where their surplus should go.
steps.consequence: The closing crew can pass it along with the baker’s consent.
steps.quote: Invite contributors to choose a home for their spare bread in advance, allowing the closing crew to pass it along with the baker's agreement.

steps.premise: A visitor may remember a bread that someone nearby knows how to bake.
steps.action: Keep a sheet for visitors to request remembered favorites.
steps.consequence: A neighbor can use a request as an idea for the next swap.
steps.quote: Keep a sheet where visitors can request a bread they remember fondly, giving a neighbor who knows how to bake it an idea for the next gathering.

steps.premise: Visitors may hesitate to make an imperfect mark in a public sketchbook.
steps.action: Invite a gardener to put an unfinished pencil study near the front.
steps.consequence: Seeing tentative lines can make visitors more comfortable drawing.
steps.quote: Let a gardener contribute an unfinished pencil study near the front. A few searching lines make putting an imperfect mark in a public book feel easier.

steps.premise: A whole garden border can be too much to fit into a sketch.
steps.action: Offer a small cardboard viewfinder.
steps.consequence: A visitor can pick a patch of stems that fits the page.
steps.quote: A small cardboard viewfinder helps someone faced with a whole border pick a patch of stems that fits on the page.

steps.premise: A visitor may need one hand for a pencil and the other to steady a child’s hand.
steps.action: Use a binding that stays open on its own.
steps.consequence: Both hands remain available for drawing together.
steps.quote: Choose a binding that lies open by itself so a visitor can hold a pencil in one hand and steady a child's hand with the other.

steps.premise: Another visitor may want to see a plant in a sketch up close.
steps.action: Leave room beside the drawing to record where the plant is in the garden.
steps.consequence: The visitor can find the plant for a closer look.
steps.quote: Leave space for the plant's garden location beside a drawing, helping another visitor track down an intriguing seed head for a closer look.

steps.premise: Other guests can enter the frame of a reference photo in a busy glasshouse.
steps.action: Ask visitors to turn the book toward the plant when taking the photo.
steps.consequence: The photo can leave other guests out of the frame.
steps.quote: Ask visitors to turn the book toward the plant when taking a reference photo, keeping other guests out of the frame in a busy glasshouse.

steps.premise: Some visitors want to try a mark privately before adding it to the shared book.
steps.action: Keep scrap paper in the pencil tray.
steps.consequence: They can test the mark before committing it to a shared page.
steps.quote: Keep a few pieces of scrap paper in the pencil tray for people who want to try a mark privately before committing it to the shared book.

steps.premise: Tomorrow’s sewer may have only the written alteration note to go on.
steps.action: Put the garment name and the side as worn on each note.
steps.consequence: The sewer can pick up the work without a demonstration.
steps.quote: Give each alteration note a garment name and the wearer's left or right side. The person sewing tomorrow should be able to pick it up without a demonstration.

steps.premise: When the room is cleared, finished pieces could get mixed into the alterations pile.
steps.action: Reserve a separate rail for stage-ready garments.
steps.consequence: Completed costumes stay out of the work still to be done.
steps.quote: Reserve a rail for garments ready to go onstage, keeping them out of the alterations pile when the room is cleared at the end.

steps.premise: A fitter needs to track time while attending to the performer.
steps.action: Put a legible clock within the fitter’s sight.
steps.consequence: They can pace the appointment without repeatedly looking away.
steps.quote: Keep an easy-to-read clock within the fitter's sight so they can pace an appointment without repeatedly looking away from the performer.

steps.premise: An owner may require a borrowed garment or its hem to be returned intact.
steps.action: Mark borrowed pieces on the rail with the owner’s limits on alterations.
steps.consequence: A volunteer can avoid making a prohibited change.
steps.quote: Mark borrowed pieces on the rail with the owner's alteration limits, saving a volunteer from shortening a hem that must be returned intact.

steps.premise: Some changes need to be checked with the wearer again.
steps.action: Circle those changes and agree on a return time while the garment and the wearer’s schedule are at hand.
steps.consequence: The team identifies the work needing a second fitting and the wearer knows when to return.
steps.quote: Circle any change that needs another fitting and agree on a return time with the wearer, while their schedule and the garment are both to hand.

steps.premise: There may be more sewing than the team can finish before a costume is needed.
steps.action: Write down the priorities the team has agreed on.
steps.consequence: A costume needed at the next day’s rehearsal gets attention in time.
steps.quote: Write down the agreed priorities if there's more sewing than the team can finish, so a costume needed at tomorrow's rehearsal gets attention in time.

steps.premise: Showing a position beside an active match can draw a crowd around the players.
steps.action: Put a demonstration board in a corner away from active games.
steps.consequence: A helper can show the position without crowding another match.
steps.quote: Place a demonstration board in a corner away from active games, giving a helper room to show a position without gathering a crowd around someone else's match.

steps.premise: A newcomer may be unsure whether a seated stranger wants an opponent.
steps.action: Offer a small sign the seated player can turn toward the door when they want a game.
steps.consequence: Visitors can tell when it is welcome to join.
steps.quote: Offer a small sign that a seated player can turn toward the door when they'd welcome an opponent, taking the guesswork out of joining a stranger.

steps.premise: When the room is busy, people may hover around games that seem nearly over.
steps.action: Use a written waiting list at busy times.
steps.consequence: Visitors can sit and read while they wait.
steps.quote: Keep a written waiting list during busy periods, letting visitors sit down to read instead of hovering over games that look nearly finished.

steps.premise: Lively post-game analysis may go on long after play ends.
steps.action: Provide a place for discussion away from the quiet boards.
steps.consequence: Players can keep analyzing while other games remain quiet.
steps.quote: Set up a place for post-game discussion a little away from the quiet boards, since a lively analysis can last much longer than the game itself.

steps.premise: A disagreement over the rules could draw in the room.
steps.action: Encourage players to speak quietly to the host when a disagreement arises.
steps.consequence: They can settle the rules question without involving everyone.
steps.quote: Encourage a quiet word with the host if a disagreement develops, giving players a way to settle a rules question without drawing in the whole room.

steps.premise: Two players may want to pause an unfinished game.
steps.action: Leave a pencil and paper to record the position.
steps.consequence: They can free the board while preserving the game for later.
steps.quote: Leave a pencil and paper for recording an unfinished position, allowing two visitors to pause a game without having to keep the board occupied.
